cuts.why: Reread ch1-cpu-p4 and p5: the ISA, assembly, and the bits of mov eax, 5 written out. Lost: the byte roles (one byte for the operation and register, four for the value), which Fig 3.1, itself now a cut candidate, also carried; both go (law 4), and byte order: 'lowest byte first' appears only in this card and its caption (ch1-cpu-p6). No later passage depends on the order of a value's bytes in memory (Fig 3.1's x86 value is one byte, Fig 3.3 reads a register, Fig 9.4 reads fields whole); p5's bit string keeps its stored order unexplained, accepted under law 4. Gap: 'opcode' is taught only in this card's strip, and a card teaches nothing, so the later unglossed uses (chBridge-trap-p1, ch7-interpret-p3's two uses, Fig BR.3's 'invalid opcode', Fig 7.7's 'dispatch to the opcode handler') are untaught either way;

Reread ch4-anatomy-p4 to p6 and p8: the two designs, the 1992 exchange and each side's point, and XNU, Android and Windows. Lost: the thread's look, and where each design runs today (microkernels in safety-critical systems, Linux in most servers, phones and supercomputers), which only its caption says. A cut adds that clause to ch4-anatomy-p8. Aliases: fig-4-1 and its caption ch4-anatomy-p7 to ch4-anatomy-p6, the paragraph before its slot.

Reread ch5-portability-p1 (1973, and recompiling replacing rewriting) and ch5-bell-labs-p1 to p3. Lost (card, caption and strip only): the 1971 First Edition still in PDP-11 assembly, moved from the PDP-7 by rewriting; the 1973 kernel only mostly in C, a small machine-dependent part left in assembly; and the 1977 port to the Interdata 8/32 by recompiling. Gap: a cut adds two sentences carrying all three after ch5-bell-labs-p3, at the card's slot, where UNIX on the PDP-7 is already introduced. Aliases: fig-5-2 and its caption ch5-bell-labs-p4 to ch5-bell-labs-p3, the paragraph before its slot.

Reread ch6-stroustrup-p2 and p3 (every date from Simula to C++98) and ch6-modern-p1 (the turn at C++11). Lost: the C++17 and C++23 notes on the timeline, the 1993 aim quote and the three-year rhythm (strip only); no prose or figure cites Fig 6.2. Gap: the three-year rhythm goes into the sentence Fig 6.9's keep adds under 'Seven standards'; the quote and the two notes go. Aliases: fig-6-2 and its caption ch6-stroustrup-p4 to ch6-stroustrup-p3, the paragraph before its slot.

Gap: a cut adds to ch7-vanrossum-p1, after the 1991 release: 'Python 3 (2008) broke compatibility with Python 2, which lived on beside it until 2020.' The rest goes. Aliases: fig-7-2 and its caption ch7-vanrossum-p3 to ch7-vanrossum-p2, the paragraph before its slot.

Reread ch16-amdahl-p3 to p5: the formula and the 20× ceiling in words. Lost: the curve flattening under 20×. Half of one idea with Fig 16.9: the serial part against a fixed job and a growing one.

<desc id="svgd-part1-6-b1-5">A slab of p-type silicon with two n-type regions, the source and the drain, and between them a gate resting on a thin insulating oxide. With the gate at 0 V there is no path. With the gate off, the free electrons (blue dots) sit in the source and drain. A positive gate voltage acts through the oxide as a field and draws them in from both sides into a thin channel under it, and they flow along it from source to drain.</desc>

<desc id="svgd-part1-6-a1-5">The same transistor twice, cut open. A slab of p-type silicon holds two n-type wells, the source and the drain, full of free electrons; above the gap between them a gate sits on a thin insulating oxide, and a wire with a lamp and a battery joins source to drain. Top, the gate at 0 V: the electrons stay in their wells, nothing joins them, and the lamp is dark. Bottom, the gate switched each cycle from 0 V to a positive voltage (1 V): its pull reaches through the oxide, electrons slide in from both wells into a thin channel under it while the holes are pushed down, current flows round the wire and the lamp lights. The gate never touches the electrons.</desc>

<svg viewBox="0 0 400 530" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="svgt-part3-30-a10-3 svgd-part3-30-a10-3" data-dur="17" data-beats="">
<title id="svgt-part3-30-a10-3">Fig 10.3 · TCP's state machine</title>
<desc id="svgd-part3-30-a10-3">Two parts, the opening above the closing, each with two lanes, the client on the left and the server on the right, and time running down. Each segment is drawn as a small packet carrying its name across the lanes. Opening: the server's program calls listen and the server waits in LISTEN; the client starts CLOSED. The client's program calls connect: it sends SYN and is in SYN_SENT; the server receives it, answers SYN-ACK and is in SYN_RCVD; the client receives that, sends ACK and is ESTABLISHED, and the server is ESTABLISHED when the ACK lands. Data flows both ways. Closing: the client's program calls close: it sends FIN and is in FIN_WAIT_1; the server receives it, acknowledges and is in CLOSE_WAIT; the ACK moves the client to FIN_WAIT_2. The server's program calls close: it sends FIN and is in LAST_ACK; the client receives it, sends the last ACK and enters TIME_WAIT, and the server is CLOSED when that ACK lands. The client waits out a timer, then is CLOSED. Each segment, call or timer moves one side one state; data moves none.</desc>

<desc id="svgd-part4-6-a13-6">Two parts.
